query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, exposure to high-temperature (>900 °C) oxidizing or corrosive environments triggers selective oxidation such that, in single-phase alloys containing barrier-forming elements (Al or Si), a coherent, adherent protective oxide layer develops and persists. In contrast, alloys that either contain Mn or exhibit a multiphase microstructure promote heterogeneous oxidation that leads to the formation of unstable oxide scales prone to cracking and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (with X = Si, Mn, or Al) prepared with controlled compositions in either a uniform single-phase solid-solution or a multiphase state.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloys to high-temperature conditions (>900 °C) in a defined oxidative or corrosive atmosphere.
generation.conditions: Isothermal treatment above 900 °C in a controlled oxidizing/corrosive environment (with fixed exposure duration and uniform heating/cooling cycles) applied equally to all alloy variants.
generation.structural_mediator: The nature of the oxide scale forming at the alloy surface — specifically, a continuous and adherent oxide enriched in Al2O3 or SiO2 in single-phase alloys versus a discontinuous, mixed oxide in Mn-containing or multiphase alloys.
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation: In single-phase alloys with high oxygen-affinity elements (Al or Si), uniform diffusion enables controlled, slow-growing oxide formation that accommodates thermal stress. In alloys with Mn or a multiphase structure, elemental segregation disrupts uniform oxidation kinetics, leading to rapid and uneven oxide growth, internal stresses, and eventual cracking/spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-temperature oxidative exposures, single-phase alloys with Al or Si will develop and maintain a thin, uniform, and adherent protective oxide layer, whereas Mn-containing or multiphase alloys will form thicker, heterogeneous oxide scales that are more likely to crack or spall.
generation.baseline: A CrFeCoNiMn or a multiphase CrFeCoNiX alloy exposed under the same conditions that is expected to form less coherent, non-protective oxide scales.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to CrFeCoNiX alloys under high-temperature (>900 °C) exposures in controlled oxidative or corrosive atmospheres. Variations in microstructural homogeneity or environmental conditions may lead to deviations in oxidation behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative differences in oxide thickness, growth rate, and mechanical integrity are uncertain without further detailed comparative studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy samples with X = Si, Mn, and Al, ensuring controlled and comparable single-phase or multiphase microstructures. Expose all samples to a high-temperature (e.g., 950 °C) oxidative or corrosive environment for a fixed duration. Characterize the resulting oxide scales using microscopy techniques (SEM/TEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase analysis, and adhesion tests (e.g., scratch or thermal cycling tests).
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and uniformity using SEM cross-section imaging
Phase composition of the oxide layer via XRD and EDS
Extent of cracking or spallation observed in adhesion tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If single-phase alloys containing Al or Si do not consistently form thinner, more uniform, and adherent oxide scales compared to Mn-containing or multiphase alloys under the same high-temperature conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX (X = Si, Mn, or Al) high-entropy alloys, the stability of a protective oxide layer above 900 °C is dictated by the selective oxidation kinetics of key alloying elements. Alloys with sufficient Cr and Al or Si favor the controlled formation of a coherent, slow-growing oxide (e.g., Cr-rich or Al/Si-rich oxide) that maintains adhesion, while higher Mn levels promote the formation of fast-growing, poorly adherent oxides that crack or spall.
drafts.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state with a defined elemental composition (variable X: Si, Mn, or Al).
drafts.intervention: Expose the alloy to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C.
drafts.conditions: Temperature >900 °C; controlled oxygen partial pressure/oxidative or corrosive environment; use of alloys with systematically varied X (Si, Mn, or Al).
drafts.structural_mediator: A coherent, adherent oxide layer (primarily Cr-rich and/or Al/Si-rich) that forms via selective oxidation at the alloy surface and whose microstructural continuity mediates long-term protection.
drafts.mechanism: The selective oxidation of high-affinity elements (Cr, and either Al or Si) forms a slow-growing, self-healing oxide. This controlled kinetics minimizes the diffusion-related stresses and thermal expansion mismatch that otherwise lead to oxide cracking. In contrast, when Mn is enriched, its rapid oxidation results in a less coherent, brittle oxide scale that is prone to spallation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Alloys with enhanced Cr and Al or Si content are expected to form a continuous, coherent protective oxide layer that resists cracking and spallation under high-temperature oxidative/corrosive conditions, whereas alloys with a higher Mn concentration will develop unstable oxide layers characterized by rapid growth, cracking, and eventual spallation.
drafts.baseline: A reference alloy with an equiatomic or balanced composition (for instance, CrFeCoNiAl) known or predicted to form a stable protective oxide, against which variations in X (Si vs Mn vs Al) are compared.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under high-temperature (>900 °C) exposures in controlled oxidative or corrosive atmospheres. Deviations in temperature, oxygen partial pressure, or significant phase segregation in multiphase alloys might alter the oxidation behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a set of CrFeCoNiX alloys with controlled variations in X composition (Si, Mn, or Al) and matched phase structure. Expose these alloys to a controlled oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures exceeding 900 °C for defined durations. Subsequently assess the oxide scale using high-resolution microscopy, phase analysis (e.g., XRD), and adhesion testing.
measurements: Phase identification of oxides (e.g., presence of Cr-rich vs. Mn-rich oxides)
Adhesion properties via spallation and cracking assessments
Elemental diffusion profiles near the oxide/alloy interface
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys with enhanced Cr and Al or Si do not form continuous, adherent oxide scales (i.e., if they exhibit similar cracking or spallation behavior as Mn-rich compositions) under the specified conditions, then the hypothesis that selective oxidation of Cr and Al/Si governs oxide stability is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high‐entropy alloys, the addition of a specific element X (Si, Mn, or Al) governs the formation and persistence of a coherent, protective oxide layer at temperatures above 900 °C by controlling the selective oxidation kinetics and interfacial bonding during scale growth. Specifically, elements that favor the formation of a slowly growing, well-adherent oxide (such as Al forming Al2O3) promote the development of a stable protective layer, whereas elements that form volatile or poorly adherent oxides (such as Mn forming Mn–rich oxides) lead to unstable scales with cracking or spallation. For Si‐containing alloys, the formation of mixed Cr–Si oxides is hypothesized to provide intermediate protection.
drafts.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys in a single-phase or multiphase metallic solid-solution state with controlled and equivalent microstructural conditions.
drafts.intervention: Exposure of the alloys to high-temperature conditions (above 900 °C) in a defined oxidative or corrosive atmosphere.
drafts.conditions: Isothermal treatment at temperatures >900 °C in an air or oxygen-rich environment (or corrosive gas mixture) for a defined duration, under otherwise identical testing conditions for each alloy composition.
drafts.structural_mediator: The nature and chemistry of the nascent oxide scale formed on the alloy surface, particularly its composition, adherence, and porosity.
drafts.mechanism: The controlled addition of X modulates the selective oxidation process: elements like Al tend to form a dense, slowly growing Al2O3 layer with low growth stress and good interfacial bonding, whereas Mn tends to form volatile or less adherent Mn-oxides that do not sustain stress relief, leading to crack initiation and scale spallation. Si, on the other hand, may induce the formation of mixed Cr-Si oxides that balance oxidation kinetics and mechanical integrity.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Alloys with Al as X will exhibit a continuous, coherent, and stable protective oxide layer at >900 °C, those with Si will show an intermediate behavior with partially protective mixed oxide scales, and those with Mn will develop unstable oxide scales that are prone to cracking or spallation, under identical exposure conditions.
drafts.baseline: The behavior of a comparable CrFeCoNi alloy without the addition of X or with a neutral X that does not significantly alter oxidation kinetics, against which the effects of adding Si, Mn, or Al are measured.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys in their single- or multiphase solid-solution state exposed to high-temperature (>900 °C) oxidative or corrosive atmospheres; deviations may be observed if the microstructure or environmental conditions change significantly.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy samples with X = Si, Mn, and Al under identical processing conditions to ensure comparable microstructures. Expose each sample to an isothermal oxidation treatment at a chosen temperature above 900 °C (e.g., 1000 °C) in a controlled, oxygen-rich atmosphere for the same duration. After exposure, characterize the oxide scales using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to assess scale continuity, composition, and evidence of cracking or spallation.
measurements: Phase and composition analysis of the oxide via XRD and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX)
Quantification of area fraction of spalled or cracked regions using image analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing alloys do not form a coherent, adherent oxide (or if the Mn-containing alloys unexpectedly form stable, spallation-free scales) under these conditions, contrary to the predicted trends, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX (X = Si, Mn, or Al) high-entropy alloys, the ability to develop and retain a stable, coherent protective oxide layer at temperatures above 900 °C is governed by the selective oxidation of barrier‐forming elements (Al and Si) that, when uniformly distributed in a single-phase solid solution, diffuse to the surface to form adherent phases (such as Al2O3 or SiO2-rich scales). In contrast, alloys with Mn or in a multiphase state experience elemental segregation that promotes the formation of heterogeneous and less coherent oxide layers, which tend to crack or spall under high-temperature oxidative or corrosive conditions.
drafts.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys prepared with controlled compositions for X = Si, Mn, or Al, in both single-phase solid-solution and multiphase states.
drafts.intervention: Expose the alloys to high-temperature conditions (above 900 °C) in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere.
drafts.conditions: Temperature >900 °C; oxidative or corrosive environment (e.g., air or oxygen-containing atmosphere); identical exposure duration and heating/cooling cycles; comparison between alloys with different X elements and between single- vs multiphase microstructures.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of a coherent, adherent oxide scale enriched in barrier-forming elements (Al2O3 or SiO2-type structures) atop a chromium-enriched sublayer, whose uniformity is compromised in multiphase or Mn-containing alloys.
drafts.mechanism: Selective oxidation driven by diffusion-controlled segregation of reactive elements. In alloys with Al or Si in a uniform (single-phase) matrix, these elements oxidize preferentially to form stable, adherent oxides. When the alloy has Mn or phase inhomogeneities, the uneven distribution of reactive elements leads to heterogeneous oxide layers that are prone to mechanical failure (cracking/spalling).
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-temperature oxidative exposure, alloys with Al or Si in a single-phase state will form thin, uniform, and adherent oxide scales that persist under test conditions, whereas Mn-containing or multiphase alloys will develop thicker, non-uniform oxides that are more likely to crack or spall.
drafts.baseline: A CrFeCoNiMn alloy in a multiphase state exposed to the same high-temperature oxidative conditions.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies to alloy exposures above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres and is relevant for comparing alloys with controlled single-phase versus multiphase microstructures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of CrFeCoNiX alloys for X = Si, Mn, and Al in both well-controlled single-phase and multiphase microstructures. Subject all samples to a standardized high-temperature exposure (e.g., 950 °C) in an oxidative environment for a fixed duration. Use scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and chemical depth profiling (e.g., EDS, XPS) to assess the uniformity, thickness, phase composition, and adhesion quality of the oxide scales formed.
measurements: Oxide scale uniformity and thickness via SEM and cross-sectional analysis
Phase composition of the oxide (detection of Al2O3, SiO2 phases vs. mixed oxides) using XRD
Adhesion and spallation behavior measured mechanically (e.g., scratch tests) and via thermal cycling
Elemental depth profiles at the alloy/oxide interface using XPS or EDS mapping
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under identical conditions, the single-phase Al- or Si-containing alloys do not consistently form thinner, more uniform, and adherent oxide scales—as evidenced by comparable or increased oxide cracking/spallation relative to Mn-containing or multiphase alloys—the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the ability to form and maintain a stable, coherent protective oxide layer when exposed to oxidative or corrosive atmospheres above 900 °C is controlled by the preferential oxidation of the selected X element. Alloys in the single-phase solid-solution state that incorporate elements with a strong oxygen affinity (such as Si or Al) will form a continuous, adherent oxide (SiO2 or Al2O3) that can accommodate thermal stresses. In contrast, alloys with X = Mn or those with a multiphase microstructure will preferentially form mixed or discontinuous oxides that are prone to cracking and spallation.
drafts.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloy prepared as either a single-phase metallic solid-solution or a multiphase solid-state mixture, with X being varied among Si, Mn, or Al.
drafts.intervention: Expose the alloy samples to an oxidizing or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures exceeding 900 °C.
drafts.conditions: Samples are held at temperatures above 900 °C (e.g., 900–1000 °C) in a controlled oxidizing and/or corrosive atmosphere for a specified duration (e.g., 100 hours) to induce oxidation.
drafts.structural_mediator: The microstructural state (single-phase versus multiphase) and the ensuing elemental partitioning at the surface that promotes the formation of either a continuous, passivating oxide (in single-phase, Si or Al-rich regions) or discontinuous, mixed oxides (in multiphase or Mn-containing alloys).
drafts.mechanism: Preferential oxidation of the X element (Si or Al) in a uniform single-phase solid-solution leads to the in situ formation of a coherent, physically adherent oxide scale (SiO2 or Al2O3) that effectively blocks further oxygen ingress and mitigates thermal expansion mismatches. In contrast, when X = Mn or if the alloy is multiphase, heterogeneities at phase boundaries favor uneven oxidation kinetics and stress localization, resulting in mixed oxides that crack or spall under thermal cycling.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Single-phase alloys containing Si or Al will develop and maintain stable, continuous oxide layers during high-temperature exposure, whereas multiphase alloys and those containing Mn will exhibit unstable, cracked, or spalled oxide layers under identical conditions.
drafts.baseline: The baseline is represented by high-entropy alloy variants that either lack the beneficial X element (or use Mn) or possess a multiphase structure, both of which are anticipated to form less coherent oxide scales that do not persist under high-temperature oxidative conditions.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies to CrFeCoNiX alloys (with X = Si, Mn, or Al) under exposure to temperatures above 900 °C in oxidizing/corrosive environments, and is primarily relevant when comparing single-phase solid-solution states against multiphase microstructures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of CrFeCoNiX alloy samples with controlled microstructures, including both single-phase (with X = Si, Al, and Mn) and intentionally produced multiphase variants. Expose all samples to an oxidizing/corrosive atmosphere maintained at temperatures above 900 °C for 100 hours. After exposure, systematically characterize the surface oxide morphology, phase composition, and adhesion using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and adhesion tests.
measurements: Continuity and adherence of the oxide layer (via SEM and adhesion tests)
Phase identification and crystallinity of the oxide scale (via XRD)
Occurrence and extent of cracks or spallation in the oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If single-phase alloys with beneficial X elements (Si or Al) do not form more coherent and adherent oxide layers than either single-phase Mn-containing or multiphase alloys, or if Mn-containing alloys unexpectedly develop a stable oxide comparable to those with Si or Al, then the hypothesis will be falsified.
